description: We're taking on the challenge, Flame in FreefalL. Using NASA's experimental data, we aim to understand how flames behave in microgravity and improve fire safety for future space missions. We're looking for members interested in programming, data analysis, and scientific research who can share ideas to one another .Together, we'll turn complex scientific data into insights for the future of space exploration.
summary:
Firetivity is a planned AI-powered web dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity fire experiments into clear safety answers. We plan to build a searchable, rankable view of investigations in NASA’s PSI database, an interactive simulator where users adjust oxygen level and airflow to see how flammability changes, and a chatbot that explains results and gives hazard assessments with citations to the original NASA data. Users will also be able to export a short report listing the sources behind each answer.
This addresses the challenge by making the data easy to find, compare, and understand, and by highlighting which research matters most for crew habitats on the Moon and Mars, where higher oxygen levels make materials burn more easily. It matters because fire is one of the deadliest risks in space, and engineers, researchers, and commercial space companies need quick, trustworthy guidance to design safer spacecraft and habitats.
details:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that turns NASA’s microgravity fire research into clear safety answers for crewed habitats.

How it works: Users pick a habitat (spacecraft, station, Moon or Mars base, rover) and a need, and the dashboard ranks 14 NASA combustion investigations by relevance, with reasons shown. A hazard simulator, built on all 129 ISS tests from BASS-II, tells users whether a material keeps burning at a given oxygen level and airflow. An AI assistant explains results in plain words, with NASA report page references. The AI only explains. The hazard rating comes from a fixed model over the real test data.

Key finding: Acrylic burned in 1.5-1.9 points leaner oxygen on the ISS than Earth screening tests suggest.

Limits: There is no Moon or Mars data in PSI yet, so we flag it and don’t guess.

Tools: [HTML/CSS/JavaScript], Vercel, [language model name], NASA PSI data. Code written with AI assistance (Anthropic Claude).
